newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Position squaring ahead of jobs.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Position squaring ahead of jobs.

text.p: Players looked for another day of limited movement in the bond market Thursday ahead of Friday's critical nonfarm payrolls report on Friday.

"We may see continued downward pressure on the market as we should see some position squaring in front of Friday's employment report. If initial jobless claims remain low that should add to the pressure," said Steve Wood, economist at BankAmerica Securities Inc.
The Labor Department was scheduled to release weekly initial jobless claims at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

No other data were scheduled for release on Thursday, but remarks from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin could have some effect. Rubin was scheduled to travel to Japan for a meeting of finance ministers and has said repeatedly this week that the U.S. would like to see any recovery of the Japanese economy be led by domestic demand, not exports.
Some saw that as a statement meant to weaken the dollar, which in turn could remove support for the Treasury market.
While most of Thursday's session should see position squaring, Wood said there may be a minor relief rally late in the day after traders had finished squaring positions.
"Lately the market only seems interested in trading on bad news. In any case, it will take a lot convincing that things are not out control," said Steven Wieting, economist at Smith Barney Inc.

Wieting said the Fed has under Chairman Alan Greenspan never moved monetary policy only once, making it illogical to assume they won't move again. The long end of the market has held up very well considering that, he said.
He also noted that 1997 had seen a lot of shifting in seasonal patterns in critical sectors such as housing due to warmer-than-usual weather.
"We could see weakness when that comes off, but it's not really a sign of fundamental weakness," Wieting said.

"The bond market is not going to do much ahead of the employment report. I'd be surprised to see a five-basis-point move in either direction," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp. "Everybody will be positioning themselves and trying to get an edge."

Johnson said the market was probably ready for a rally, but it would take a reading below 180,000 new jobs in the payrolls report and average hourly earnings growth of less than 0.3 percent for that to occur.
Economists at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. expressed concern about Friday's employment report while calling for a payrolls rise of 150,000.

"Typically, NAPM employment indices greater than 48 are associated with 200,000-person or more increases in payroll employment (the NAPM employment index for March was 51.6). We are also very concerned about the wage component," the economists said. "We estimate it to be up 0.3 percent but would not be surprised to see a stronger wage component."
DLJ economists said the wage component would prove most important in upcoming formulations of monetary policy.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, weekly jobless claims would come in at 310,000 on Thursday, the same level as last week.

Late Wednesday the 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 94-12/32 to yield 7.08 percent. The 10-year was at 95-19/32 to yield 6.87 percent. The five-year was at 99-19/32 to yield 6.72 percent and the two-year was at 99-23/32 to yield 6.40 percent.
Three-month bills were at 5.15 percent; six-month bills at 5.30 percent and year bills at 5.64 percent.
